power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: The role of climate and immunity in Brazil's unprecedented outbreak of dengue in 2024

text.text: Brazil experienced a large dengue epidemic during the 2024 season, with almost 5.7 million total cases (compared to under 1.3 million in 2023), raising questions about underlying drivers, including rising temperatures, expansion into susceptible populations, changes in reporting, and novel strains.
We compared state-level 2024 incidence with 2000-2023 data to quantify anomalies.
Nine of 27 states, primarily in the Southeast, recorded their highest incidence in 25 years, accounting for 97% of cases while comprising only 67% of the population.
In contrast, nine states (mostly in the North and Northeast) reported below-average incidence.

Counterintuitively, the correlation between state-level temperature and incidence declined significantly over the study period, turning negative by 2024 (r = -0.72), a reversal from the positive correlations observed at the start.

To determine whether this pattern was driven by northern temperatures being too high for transmission, or by spatial variation in immunity, we fit generalized additive models to effective reproductive numbers.
Transmission remained substantial at the highest temperatures, while reproductive numbers declined with lagged cumulative incidences, indicating susceptibility depletion was important.

We then estimated state-level susceptibility using a mechanistic SEIR-SEI model, describing a trade-off: high temperatures supported high transmission rates, but were associated with reduced susceptibility.

Linear regression models confirmed both temperature and susceptibility were necessary to predict the 2024 outbreaks, suggesting that immunity plays an important role in modulating temperature's effect on incidence.
Future surveillance integrating measures of immunity could enhance forecasts and early-warning systems, particularly as climate change expands dengue into immunologically naïve populations.
Brazil experienced an unprecedented dengue epidemic in 2024, with nearly 5.7 million reported cases.
The relative role of high temperature and population immunity in driving this large outbreak remains poorly understood.
High temperatures are known to support increased transmission but surprisingly, the relationship between incidence and temperature had turned negative by this outbreak.
Our results show that transmission remained viable at the highest temperatures, but outbreaks were constrained by immunity acquired through prior infection.
Large epidemics occurred only where favorable temperatures coincided with high remaining susceptibility, itself largely a legacy of past, temperature-driven transmission.

text.text: The number of reported dengue cases worldwide more than doubled from 2023 to 2024 1 .

text.text: This increase was in part driven by the largest epidemic ever recorded in the Americas with Brazil reporting almost 5.7 million suspected cases, representing 79% of the total in the Americas.
Transmission is endemic in large parts of Brazil and large-scale outbreaks have occurred regularly; however, the 2024 outbreak was unprecedented.
Of all hypotheses being proposed to explain Brazil's unprecedented 2024 dengue outbreak, climate change is the most common.
An El Niño event increased temperatures and altered rainfall, increasing mosquito density and expanding the vector's range 1, 2 .

text.text: Mechanistic models based on mosquito thermal physiology predict that basic reproductive numbers (R0) increase nonmonotonically with temperature, reaching a peak before declining at higher temperatures 3, 4 .

text.text: These temperature-dependent R0 curves have been used to project future expansion of suitable habitat and epidemic potential under climate change 3, 5, 6 .

text.text: More recently, a global analysis found dengue incidence to similarly depend nonlinearly on temperature 7 .

text.text: The nonlinear effects of temperature, combined with the multiplicative nature of transmission dynamics, means that even modest increases in temperature could lead to disproportionate case surges.
In addition to climate, other contributing factors, many related to immunity, have been put forward.

Serotype dynamics may have created local gaps in immunity: the co-circulation of multiple serotypes 8 , the re-emergence of DENV-3 in São Paulo [8] [9] [10] , and the DENV-2 Cosmopolitan genotype into the Western Amazon 11 all placed populations with limited serotype-specific immunity at greater risk.

text.text: Increased human mobility may also have facilitated introduction into new areas.
Urbanization and deforestation in the Central-West and Southeast may have expanded Aedes aegypti breeding sites 13, 14 , exposing populations with low immunity.

text.text: Other factors unrelated to immunity have also been proposed: co-circulating arboviruses with similar symptoms (e.g., Oropouche, chikungunya, and Zika) have posed challenges to surveillance and likely inflated suspected dengue counts [15] [16] [17] [18] , while differences in reporting may have contributed to the elevated counts observed in 2024.

text.text: Climate change and immunity are often examined in isolation, with less attention given to how they may interact spatially.
As climates warm, areas transition from unsuitable to suitable for sustained transmission, exposing fully susceptible populations to dengue.

As seen in pandemics, initial outbreaks of immunizing pathogens in such populations greatly exceed subsequent outbreaks, as initial large outbreaks induce immunity that reduces or blunts future transmission.

A recent exploratory analysis of municipality-level dengue incidence and temperature in Brazil observed a shift from a positive correlation in 2013 to a negative correlation in 2024, with population immunity proposed as a potential driver of this change. 19 Other authors have highlighted the expansion of dengue into areas with low historical transmission as possible drivers of incidence in recent years 20, 21 , but often the focus is on the impact of temperature on mosquito abundance and transmission alone 1, 2, [22] [23] [24] .

text.text: To investigate the drivers of Brazil's 2024 dengue epidemic, we analyzed 24 years of state and municipality-level case and temperature data.

A striking pattern observed in Brazil requires explanation: many northern states with consistently high temperatures (previously associated with higher dengue transmission) experienced average or below-average case counts, while southeastern states with comparatively lower temperatures, saw unprecedented outbreaks.
We fit models to quantify the importance of temperature and population immunity in explaining the 2024 outbreak and its spatial patterns.

Using a mechanistic, temperature-dependent transmission model, we inferred state-level susceptibility indices, and tested whether accounting for spatial variation in immunity could resolve the apparent contradiction between temperature and incidence patterns.

Our study addresses how climate-driven range expansion interacts with immunity dynamics to shape dengue emergence and outbreaks, insights that have implications for anticipating future outbreaks as warming continues.

text.text: Nevertheless, to test these hypotheses while accounting for epidemic dynamics, we estimated weekly reproductive numbers (Rt) for each state using time series of weekly cases, and then fit a generalized additive model (GAM) with temperature as a smooth predictor.
This approach allows us to detect whether and to what extent transmission declines at high temperatures.
We found that Rt increased with temperature up to 28.4°C (95% CI: 27.9 -28.9°C; solid line in the top panel of Fig. 3), and decreased thereafter.

text.text: Though Rt decreased with temperatures increasing above 28.4°C, we found that they remained high (for example, Rt at 32°C was higher than 70% (95% CI: 66 -75) of observed values across the country and time).

Notably, when the fitted temperature response is evaluated at each two-week window of the 2024 season and averaged across the season, its contribution to log(Rt) was higher for the northern and northeastern states (+0.08 to +0.11 for Amapá, Roraima, Amazonas, Piauí, Ceará, and Maranhão) than for São Paulo (-0.09), reflecting the north's sustained near-optimal temperatures through most of the year versus São Paulo's briefer warm season.

Temperature alone would therefore predict greater transmission potential in the north than in São Paulo, making it difficult to attribute the north's comparatively modest 2024 incidence to thermal suppression.
Note, however, that it is at the extremes where there is least data to inform the decline in Rt with precision.

Given that the fitted temperature contribution to log(Rt), averaged across two-week windows of the 2024 season, was higher in the northern and northeastern states listed above than in São Paulo, we next asked whether historical incidence could explain variation in transmission through the accumulation of immunity.
We incorporated cumulative incidence at multiple time scales (within each season and over our entire dataset) as proxies for susceptible depletion.
We found clear decreases in Rt as cumulative incidence increased at both timescales, supporting a strong role for susceptibility (Fig. 3).

text.text: At the time of introduction, when populations are fully susceptible, the correlation starts positive.
However, as susceptibles are rapidly depleted in warmer northern states but not in cooler southern states, later outbreaks shift southward, despite the lower temperatures.
This causes the correlation to turn negative (the timing of the sign change depends on whether mean temperatures remain constant or increase linearly).
Once susceptibles are also depleted in southern states, the correlation returns to positive.
Similarly, a sharp increase in mean temperature across all states (due to, e.g., an unusually warm year) can also cause a positive correlation to temporarily turn negative (SI Appendix, Fig. S6).

text.text: In contrast, removing spatial variation in temperatures and thus in immunity (assuming similarly high temperatures throughout Brazil) causes the correlation to turn negative just after dengue introduction, but it returns to positive much sooner, and remains positive throughout the simulation for most parameters explored.

These simulations show that the shifting temperature-incidence correlation observed in Brazil may arise from spatial variation in immunity that results from spatial variation in temperature, rather than from temperature's direct effect on transmission alone.

Our GAM analysis, which revealed strong dependencies between reproductive numbers, temperature, and proxies for immunity, is a phenomenological approach that cannot distinguish how temperature affects transmission (whether directly, via effects on the thermal biology of the vector, or indirectly, through past transmission shaping immunity levels).

text.text: Brazil experienced an unprecedented dengue season in 2024, coinciding with record high mean temperatures across much of the country.

This prompted climate change to be proposed as a primary cause, yet the largest outbreaks occurred in southeastern states with comparatively lower temperatures than northern states (Fig. 1), culminating in the shift to negative spatial correlations (Fig. 2).

text.text: We show this apparent contradiction is explained by spatial variation in population immunity: the 2024 surge resulted from an increasingly suitable climate interacting with areas of high susceptibility.

Significant clusters of incidence anomalies aligned with states we inferred as having relatively high susceptibility (e.g., São Paulo, Minas Gerais, Distrito Federal), while states in the North and Northeast, which also experienced warming, had lower susceptibility and reported more limited outbreaks (SI Appendix, Fig. S8).

text.text: The significant interaction between temperature and susceptibility suggests that temperature's association with incidence is modulated by susceptibility: the effect of temperature is greater with high levels of susceptibility, and similarly, the effect of susceptibility on incidence is greater at higher temperatures.
The observed shift from positive to negative fitted correlations between incidence and temperature could serve as a signature of range expansion into immunologically naive populations.
The relationship between dengue incidence and temperature is mediated by immunity, and can be expected to evolve, from when a virus is initially introduced, to endemicity.

In the initial phases post-introduction to climatically suitable areas and immunologically naive populations, a positive correlation between incidence and temperature might be expected, though some variability may arise due to differences in the timing of introduction of DENV to new areas.
However, as susceptible hosts are depleted in these optimal environments, the spatial patterns of incidence would change.
Climate-driven expansion of the vector's range into new, immunologically naive areas, particularly large metropolitan centers, could compound this effect.

Together, these processes would lead to an increasingly heterogeneous immune landscape where low susceptibility blunts outbreaks despite more optimal temperatures, resulting in the observed negative correlations.
In the future, as dengue becomes endemic and Brazil becomes more immunologically homogeneous, we might expect the correlation between temperature and incidence to become positive again.
The role of population immunity in explaining dengue outbreaks is often overlooked, but crucial given the role played by range expansion in the 2024 outbreak in Brazil.

text.text: The results are compatible because they answer different questions.

Childs et al. estimate an effect averaged across many endemic locations and years, not a single year or spatial anomaly, and attribute the immunity-invariance to endemic populations never reaching persistent herd immunity, through waning and serotype turnover.
The 2024 outbreak in Brazil points to the opposite case: large populations with lower historical transmission undergoing a range expansion.
This is a scenario their analysis explicitly sets aside.

Consistent with this, our analyses suggest that accounting for immunity greatly improves predictions of the spatial patterns of the 2024 outbreak Defining R0, and especially the conditions that define the critical transmission threshold R0 = 1, remains critical for predicting dengue incidence.

However, mechanistic expressions for the temperature dependence of R0 usually assume stationarity 28 , and rely on variables that are difficult to estimate in the field and are expected to be spatially heterogeneous, such as the vector-to-host ratio (on which R0 depends; see SI Appendix, Appendix S2).

text.text: This limitation bears directly on why the Southeast surged in 2024 and not earlier: without an absolute estimate of R0, we cannot identify whether or when its transmission potential first crossed the R0 = 1 threshold for sustained transmission, and so cannot fully account for the timing of the outbreak.

It is also possible that preceding years saw widespread but largely unreported transmission (primary dengue infections are frequently mild or asymptomatic) with part of the 2024 reported surge reflecting secondary, more often symptomatic infections in populations primed in the year(s) before.
Our findings are subject to several limitations.

Surveillance biases likely distorted incidence data: the misclassification of Oropouche virus (OROV) or Chikungunya cases as dengue in the South (e.g., Santa Catarina) may have inflated reported incidence, while systemic underreporting of DENV-3 in the Northeast may have masked earlier resurgences, thereby skewing our susceptibility estimates for these regions 9, 15 .

Our estimates of reproductive numbers assume a fixed generation interval, which instead would be expected to vary with temperature 29, 30 .

text.text: Our modeling framework makes several simplifying assumptions.

The single-serotype SEIR-SEI model does not account for serotypespecific immunity; our 'initial susceptibility index' is therefore an aggregate measure that may mask complex inter-serotype immune dynamics.
Because each state-season is fit independently, with no constraint linking successive seasons, a serotype introduction that reset susceptibility would be absorbed as a jump in 𝑆 !"
& ; the fit is agnostic as to whether a given shift reflects a serotype introduction, demographic turnover, or waning cross-protection.

text.text: We have not addressed several alternative mechanisms that could have contributed to the pattern of dengue observed in 2024 in Brazil.
Introduction of new serotypes into some areas may have contributed to greater levels of incidence.

text.text: These observations caution against assuming uniform serotype circulation across Brazil, but do not support large spatial differences across Brazil in serotypes circulating.
The contribution of pre-existing immunity to higher rates of apparent illness was not explicitly addressed here, though could also contribute to variation.

Finally, differences in reporting, though estimated in our models and not found to contribute to systematic differences in cases in southern states compared to northern states, could contribute to differences in incidence.
All analyses were conducted at the state level.

We chose this scale because over a third of Brazil's municipalities have a median of zero cases per season (five or fewer, for almost two-thirds), and 39% of all municipality-seasons record zero cases, a degree of sparsity that destabilizes both reproductive-number estimation and susceptibility inference.

Confounding requires that an omitted factor be correlated with temperature: sub-state heterogeneity in incidence that is uncorrelated with temperature cannot bias the state-level association, and averaging over many such independent local departures suppresses their contribution to the state-level estimate.

The risk aggregation cannot address is heterogeneity that is correlated with temperature at the sub-state level, e.g., municipality-level gradients in reporting rate or vector-control investment that correlate with local climate, which could bias the state-level associations in either direction.

The Rt GAMs include state and season fixed effects, which absorb time-invariant between-state differences and nationwide inter-seasonal variation, but not state-specific time-varying confounds or sub-state heterogeneity.
The correlation analysis (Fig. 2) and the regression models (Fig. 5) make no such adjustment, because the between-state contrast is itself the quantity of interest.

text.text: We therefore cannot rule out residual confounding at the state level.

Moving to a municipality scale would not in itself resolve this: separating such confounding from the associations of interest would still require either measured covariates for the suspected confounds (health-system capacity, vector-control measures, reporting rates), or a design that removes variation at the confound's own scale (e.g., within-municipality, over time), which reintroduces the data sparsity that motivated the state-level choice in the first place.

In inferring the initial susceptibility index, we also assumed a spatiotemporally uniform vector-to-host ratio, reporting rate, and number of infections introduced to each location at the start of a season, which are significant oversimplifications.

Spatial differences in vector control act through the vector-to-host ratio: historically low-burden states such as São Paulo may never have built the dengue-specific control capacity of more affected states, and any such difference would be absorbed into the susceptibility index, producing a spatial pattern much like the one we attribute to immunity.

We therefore treat the susceptibility index as a relative rather than absolute measure of population susceptibility, a use supported by the stability of indices within and across states when estimated from total versus confirmed cases, despite their substantially different reporting rates (SI Appendix, Fig. S7).

text.text: The assumptions made in these compartmental models also lead to unrealistically fast dynamics, potentially inconsistent with spatial heterogeneity within states, making the estimation of susceptibility more difficult.
Finally, beyond the inherent assumptions of our SEIR-SEI model, we highlight three potential temperature-related biases.

First, the temperature dependence of vector life-history traits, derived from laboratory experiments under constant conditions, may bias rate estimates in fluctuating real-world temperatures, with the expected bias dependent on the response functions' curvature at a given temperature 31 .

text.text: Second, the gridded temperature dataset we use here is interpolated and averaged over relatively large spatiotemporal scales, which may not reflect the microclimatic temperatures actually experienced by mosquitoes, nor the precise temperatures in the laboratory experiments used to parameterize the model.

Third, as demonstrated by Childs et al. 7 , temperature datasets can also exhibit significant discrepancies for a given location, potentially leading to substantial variations in estimated vital rates solely based on the dataset used.

text.text: We used total reported dengue cases in our analyses, which may introduce biases due to misclassification of other febrile illnesses.
However, when we repeated analyses using only confirmed cases, results remained qualitatively unchanged (see SI Appendix, Appendix S3).

text.text: Confirmed cases have their own limitations: there can be less testing during large epidemics due to resource constraints, potentially leading to greater underreporting in high-incidence years and states.

Thus, while neither measure is perfect, the consistency of results across both definitions strengthens confidence that the spatial and temporal patterns we identify, particularly with regards to the roles of temperature and immunity, likely reflect true epidemiological dynamics rather than surveillance biases.
As noted above, we do not distinguish between primary and secondary infections, limiting our ability to project past 2024.
The 2024 outbreak in southeastern states could constrain transmission through accumulated immunity.
However, populations with monotypic immunity remain vulnerable to secondary infections, which could lead to increased cases if other serotypes were to circulate in the near future.

At the same time, continued range expansion into southern states (Paraná, Santa Catarina, and Rio Grande do Sul), and potentially other large, immunologically naive metropolitan areas like Buenos Aires, could drive substantial future outbreaks.
Our results suggest avenues for further research to improve our understanding of the spatiotemporal evolution of dengue epidemics in emerging and re-emerging settings.

First, reconstruction of population susceptibility even at crude scales (e.g., statewide and annual) will provide information about areas at risk of increased transmission and with higher sensitivity to climatic changes.

This reconstruction could be achieved using case data where available 32 , bolstered by population representative serological surveys 27, 33 , although methodological development is necessary to integrate data sources and project these estimates countrywide.

text.text: Second, our models using reconstructed susceptibility indices outperformed models using mean temperature, suggesting that current models using temperature-dependent reproductive numbers to predict changes in dengue transmission would also benefit from integration of susceptibility estimates informed by transmission models.
One step towards this could be the use of effective reproductive numbers in assessing climate associations (rather than incidence) as this accounts, at least in part, for changes in susceptibility.
Consideration of population immunity will likely also be critical in improving the accuracy and increasing the time horizon of models forecasting dengue burden, as noted by Wu et al. 34 .

text.text: Whether a measure of immunity is needed for prediction in other settings will depend on regime: it is likely to matter most during susceptibility regime shifts such as range expansions into newly suitable areas, or in the aftermath of a serotype introduction or unusually large outbreaks, and least where susceptibility is more stable, as in long-established endemic areas.
Our results also note the weakness of using only historical case numbers to project future burden.

Integration of historical climate and estimates of immunity (including serotype specific estimates) into forecast models would represent significant progress in this field and increase the value of these models to public health.
We conducted a retrospective ecological time-series analysis to investigate the drivers of the 2024 dengue epidemic in Brazil.
Our analysis compared state-level incidence, temperature, and their 2024 season anomalies against a 23-year historical baseline (2001-2023).

To quantify the relationship between temperature and incidence, we calculated Pearson's correlation coefficients (r) and associated 95% confidence intervals, across states (one value per state), between (i) the 2024 season temperature anomalies and the 2024 incidence anomalies, and To summarize how the season-by-season correlation series changed over time, we regressed the coefficients on season by generalized least squares on the Fisher-z scale (atanh r), with inversevariance weights and a first-order autoregressive term across seasons, to account for the coefficients' unequal uncertainty and serially correlated residuals.
Trend slopes are reported as the change in atanh r per year; fitted values are back-transformed to the correlation scale for Fig. 2.

text.text: To understand how spatiotemporal patterns in dengue cases in Brazil are related to temperature and population susceptibility, we first analyzed an outcome of estimated effective reproductive numbers (Rt) derived from reported case data.

Rt are more robust to differences in reporting than raw case numbers, and reflect a combination of transmissibility and population immunity (Rt=R0*St, where St is the proportion of the population susceptible).

Reproductive numbers were calculated using the EpiEstim v2.2.5 41 package in R from weekly state-level time series of cases over a twoweek moving window, assuming a mean serial interval of 12 days and a standard deviation of 3 days.
text.formatted: Reproductive numbers were calculated using the EpiEstim v2.2.5 <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">41</ref> package in R from weekly state-level time series of cases over a twoweek moving window, assuming a mean serial interval of 12 days and a standard deviation of 3 days.

text.text: Estimates based on fewer than five cases within a window were deemed unreliable and excluded from subsequent analysis, and Rt values equal to or greater than 10 were also deemed unreliable and excluded (as they were often estimated for the start of the time period, or in states that reported few cases).

The log-transformed Rt values were the dependent variable in a generalized additive model (GAM) from the mgcv v1.9.4 package 42 in R. The GAM included a smooth term for mean temperature for the same two-week moving window, and smooth terms for the lag-1 log-cumulative incidence per 100,000 (both within-season and overall, state-level) as a proxy for the build-up of immunity prior to the time window over which Rt was estimated, and thus accounting for changing susceptibility driven by annual outbreak dynamics and historical transmission.

We used a contemporaneous temperature window rather than distributed lags deliberately: the aim is to isolate temperature's direct effect on transmission from its lagged, indirect effect through accumulated immunity, which the cumulative-incidence terms (themselves a historical function of temperature) already capture.
Adding lagged temperature would induce collinearity between it and the lagged incidences, blurring this decomposition.
More fundamentally, a temperature lag cannot represent the path-dependent depletion of susceptibles -whether an outbreak actually occurred -that the cumulative incidence terms carry.
We note that "direct" is approximate here, since temperatures ultimately act on mosquito life history at multiple lags.
Season and state were included as categorical fixed effects.
To assess the relationship between temperature and Rt when not accounting for historic incidence, the same model was fit excluding the cumulative incidence smooth terms.
To minimize the risk of overfitting, the GAM was fitted with double penalization and the smoothing parameter estimation was made using restricted maximum likelihood.
To further reduce the risk of overfitting, we performed 10-fold cross-validation to select the optimal basis dimension (k) from a range of 3 to 30 (the same value used across all smooth terms).
To account for temporal autocorrelation in the residuals, models were fitted using the 'bam' function with an AR(1) error structure.
The autocorrelation parameter ρ was estimated from the mean lag-1 autocorrelation of residuals from an initial model fit, calculated separately for each state-year series.
Performance was measured by the RMSE and Pearson correlation coefficient between predicted and observed values on the out-of-sample data.
